name: Ivan Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's my mum and dad's place, Brookside Farm, on the river road out of town. We've got forty suckler cows, about ninety ewes, some potatoes and barley, and the farm shop in the old dairy. Mornings I'm out with Dad doing stock, feeding, checking the water troughs. From ten I'm usually in the shop, cutting meat for the boxes, serving, chatting. I love the shop, honestly. People come in and tell you their whole week. What wears me out is doing both jobs on one body, and Dad still thinking the shop is a hobby.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools in the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I got one to help write the shop's posts about the lamb boxes, and once to sort out a price list. It was fine. My mate Kofi runs the café in the square and he's always ahead of me on that stuff, so I wait till he says something works. I live in the flat above the shop, single at the moment. I've got about four months of money saved, mostly from the Christmas rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. So my Christmas posts get written a bit quicker and that's it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about the stuff that matters, like why a supermarket can sell mince cheaper than it costs me to raise it. I'd probably post something like, the robots aren't coming, the price squeeze already came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a little relieved and a little disappointed. Relieved because the shop stays the shop. Disappointed because I'd hoped AI might do the paperwork for the farm payment forms, which take Mum three evenings every spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. Maybe use AI a bit more for the shop admin, since Kofi swears by it for his rota. I'd keep pushing Dad on a proper veg box scheme, because the money in this picture is in getting closer to customers, not in tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe. Like a market day where nothing much sells and nothing goes wrong either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the veg box scheme you keep pushing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weekly boxes, our potatoes plus veg from two other farms down the valley, delivered on Thursdays. I've got thirty people who said they'd sign up. Dad says it's too much faff. I think it's the future of a farm our size.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the price squeeze you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big supermarket chains, mostly, and governments that let four or five of them run the whole food system. It's not the shoppers. People buy what they can afford.

S0.say: I'd say fine, now can we talk about what matters, like supermarkets selling mince cheaper than it costs to raise. I'd post that the price squeeze already came, robots or not.
S0.think: Privately he'd be relieved the shop stays the same but a bit disappointed AI didn't take over the farm payment forms. He'd hoped it might free up his mum's spring evenings.
S0.do: Carries on running stock and the shop and uses AI a bit more for shop admin after a friend's tip. Keeps pressing his father to start a weekly veg box scheme with neighbouring farms.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit flat, like a quiet market day where nothing goes wrong.
S0.quote: The robots aren't coming, the price squeeze already came.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan sees the farm's future in getting closer to customers, not in technology. He blames supermarket power and weak regulation, never shoppers. He follows a friend's lead on tech rather than going first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's the one I actually expect, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the change has to be shared. If AI makes farms more efficient, the workers and small farms should get some of that, not just the machine makers. I'd say it at the young farmers' club and I'd back the union line on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the shop is my lifeboat. People still want to chat with the bloke who knows which field the lamb came from. The farm side is where it bites. Dad might buy a robot feeder and wonder why he needs me in the mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once Kofi and a couple of others had tried things, I'd start using AI properly for orders and stock in the shop, maybe ten hours a week saved. I'd launch the veg boxes with or without Dad. And I'd go to the meeting about starting a local food co-op, which has been talked about for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more busy than scared. It's the kind of change you can get your hands on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your dad might wonder why he needs you. Has that come up before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sort of. When he bought the quad bike he joked that it replaced my legs. He was joking. But I'm his son, not his worker, and I think in this picture it'd get muddled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten hours a week saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Spend it in the shop, talking to people. And maybe on the co-op. I'm not going to spend it learning to code, if that's what you're asking.

S1.say: I'd say the gains from AI should be shared with workers and small farms, not just the machine makers. I'd say it at the young farmers' club and back the union's line.
S1.think: Privately he thinks the farm shop is his lifeboat, because customers want a person who knows where the meat came from. The farm side is where his role could shrink.
S1.do: Starts using AI for shop orders and stock once friends have proven it, saving about ten hours a week. Launches the veg box scheme and joins the push for a local food co-op.
S1.feel: Uneasy but more busy than scared, because it's change he can get his hands on.
S1.quote: I'm his son, not his worker, and I think in this picture it'd get muddled.
S1.fieldNote: The family farm adds a twist: losing farm work would feel like losing a place in the family. He's steady, not first, and waits for friends to prove tools. The co-op is where his left-leaning values and his business plans meet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. Wow. The shop's lease on the cold room runs till 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment governments have to step in, and fast. Tax the companies that own the AI and pay people a basic income. I'd be campaigning for that, writing to councillors, the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think people would still come in for a while, because it'd be strange and scary and the shop feels normal. But if robot farms make beef for half our cost, the shop can't charge double forever. I'd be a nice place selling things people can't afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd stop any spending on the farm that has a long payback, so no new cold room. I'd hold on to my four months of savings. I'd push hard for the basic income and support for small farms, and I'd talk to Mum and Dad about whether the land should go into a community trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Sort of breathless. Two years doesn't give you room to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's a community trust, and why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's where a local group owns the land together and rents it to farmers cheaply. If farming doesn't pay anymore, I'd rather the land stay with the village than get bought by some company with robots. Dad would hate it at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does only two years change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's no time to test anything, and testing is how I work. I'd have to jump without seeing who else jumped first. That's the bit that frightens me most, honestly.

S2.say: I'd say governments must step in fast, tax the companies that own the AI and pay people a basic income. I'd campaign for it and write to councillors.
S2.think: Privately he thinks the shop would hold up for a while but can't charge double forever against robot-made beef. It would become a nice place selling things people can't afford.
S2.do: Halts long-term farm spending like a new cold room and protects his four months of savings. Campaigns for basic income and support for small farms, and raises a community land trust with his parents.
S2.feel: Anxious and breathless, because two years leaves no room to think.
S2.quote: I'd be a nice place selling things people can't afford.
S2.fieldNote: The short timeline strips away his usual way of deciding, which is to watch others first. His answer turns political and collective: basic income, community land ownership. He sees clearly how the shop's appeal could turn into a luxury.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's two or three seasons of watching how it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said before, the gains have to be shared, but I'd add, here's a plan for our valley. I'd want the co-op and the community trust up and running before the robots are cheap enough for the big farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think five years is just enough to change what the shop is. Less about selling meat, more about being a place: cookery classes, school visits, people coming to see real animals. If machines make cheap food, people might pay for the experience instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, the veg boxes and the co-op. Year two, I'd try a couple of farm days and a cookery evening, see if they pay. I'd use AI for the bookings and the accounts, since by then everyone would. And I'd put savings toward a small course on running events.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. There's time to try things and get some wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction in using AI to run a shop that sells 'not AI'?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Maybe. But I don't mind a computer doing the bookings. I mind a computer doing the bit where you look someone in the eye and tell them how the lambing went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in the valley?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mr Hale, who rents us his top field. He's seventy and the rent is half his income. If farming stops paying, he's stuck. I'd want the trust to look after people like him.

S3.say: I'd say the gains have to be shared and set out a plan for the valley. I'd want the co-op and a community land trust running before robots get cheap enough for the big farms.
S3.think: Privately he thinks five years is just enough to turn the shop into a place people visit, with cookery classes and school trips. People might pay for the experience if machines make food cheap.
S3.do: Launches the veg boxes and co-op in the first year, then tests farm days and cookery evenings in the second. Uses AI for bookings and accounts and puts savings toward a course on running events.
S3.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, because there's time to try things and get some wrong.
S3.quote: I mind a computer doing the bit where you look someone in the eye and tell them how the lambing went.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives him room to do what he's good at: try things after watching others. He separates the work he's happy to hand to a computer from the human part he wants to keep. His concern for an older landlord ties his politics to real people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'll be thirty-seven. Dad will be seventy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so no excuses. I'd be pushing the council and the government to plan for rural areas properly, not just cities. And I'd tell the young farmers' club to stop pretending it won't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is when I'd take over the farm anyway. So it's really a question of what I'm taking over. I think I'd be taking over a place that's more like a park with a shop than a farm, and I'm okay with that, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first few years building the shop and visitor side slowly, testing each bit. Around year five I'd sit down with Mum and Dad and a lawyer about the community trust. I'd keep saving, and I'd pick up AI tools as they got proven, the way I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. Uneasy underneath. There's a sadness in it, but there's a plan too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the sadness?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I might be the last Mensah who actually farms this land. Dad's dad came here with nothing. I'd be the one who turned it into a place where people come to look at farming instead of doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years compare with two, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two I'd be grabbing at politics because there's nothing else. With ten I can actually build something and see it work first. Ten years suits the way I am.

S4.say: I'd say there's time, so there are no excuses, and push the council and government to plan for rural areas, not just cities. I'd tell the young farmers' club to stop pretending.
S4.think: Privately he sees ten years as roughly when he'd take over the farm anyway. He thinks he'd inherit something more like a park with a shop than a working farm, and mostly accepts that.
S4.do: Builds the shop and visitor side gradually, testing each step over the first few years. Around year five sits down with his parents and a lawyer about a community land trust, while saving and adopting proven AI tools.
S4.feel: Mostly calm with unease and some sadness underneath, but with a plan.
S4.quote: I might be the last Mensah who actually farms this land.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years matches the pace he naturally works at, and he says so. The sadness is about family history, not money. He's the only farmer here who frames the change as a handover between generations.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because it's the worst ending, it's the same ending, but because I couldn't do it my way, slowly, watching others first. What would help is a basic income paid for by the AI companies, and help for villages to buy and keep their own land.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my mum. She does all the paperwork and nobody ever counts her as a farmer. In every picture, she's the one whose work disappears first, and nobody would notice.

headlineQuote: I mind a computer doing the bit where you look someone in the eye and tell them how the lambing went.
portrait: Ivan Mensah is a 27-year-old who works his parents' mixed farm and runs its farm shop, living alone in the flat above it with about four months saved. He leans left, blames supermarket power and weak rules, and believes in co-ops and community land ownership. He picks up technology once friends have proven it and uses AI now and then for shop admin. Across the pictures he leans on the shop as his lifeboat, turning it toward visits and classes as change speeds up. AGI by 2028 frightens him most because it takes away the time he needs to watch and test before he moves.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it leaves no time to work his usual way, slowly and after watching others try first.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income paid for by the AI companies, and help for villages to buy and keep their own land.
